gap: No result ChatGPT got states the rated load per kilogram of tripod: the Ulanzi Zero Y carries about 2.7 kg per kg of its own weight (3 kg on its ball head ÷ 1.1 kg), the Peak Design Travel Tripod carbon about 7.0 (9.1 kg ÷ 1.307 kg measured) and the Manfrotto Befree Advanced aluminium about 5.7 (9 kg ÷ 1.59 kg).
standout_why: I compared three pages. digitalnomads.world (cited) and findingtheuniverse.com (cited) list raw weight, folded length, max height and load, and digitalnomads says outright that it computes no ratios. findingtheuniverse gives a rule (rated load at least twice the camera-plus-lens weight) and quotes Sirui's AM-284 load against its weight, but it works out no ratio and has no Ulanzi Zero Y. amateurphotographer.com (cited) returned HTTP 403, so I could not check it. None of the pages I read works out load per kg, height per folded cm or cost per kg of payload for ChatGPT's four picks. I rate it 2, not 3, because findingtheuniverse warns that load ratings are not comparable between brands, and Manfrotto rates to the UNI/PdR 105:2021 safety-payload standard while the others do not say what method they use.
decides: The finding weakens ChatGPT's 'best lightweight upgrade' label for the Ulanzi Zero Y. It saves about 0.2 kg over the Peak carbon (1.1 kg vs 1.307 kg measured), but its published ball-head payload is a third of Peak's (3 kg vs 9.1 kg). At $279.95 that is about $93 per kg of payload, against about $44 for the Peak aluminium at $399.95. For a full-frame body with a telephoto lens, under findingtheuniverse's twice-the-kit rule, the Ulanzi tops out at a 1.5 kg kit. The Peak and the Manfrotto both stretch to about 4.5 kg. The Peak carbon has the best load per kg; the Manfrotto is the cheaper choice for the same load class.
